subsection: 8. Images of Ireland: film, music, tourism and heritage, and John F. Kennedy

notes.h: Why images of Ireland were made abroad
notes.b: After 1840 emigration created large Irish communities abroad, so Ireland was imagined overseas as much as it was lived at home. Films, songs and tourism were the main ways those images were made and passed on.
points: Emigration from 1840 built a large Irish community in the USA, Britain, Canada and Australia, so many people of Irish descent knew Ireland only through stories, songs and films rather than through daily life.

Irish America was mainly Catholic and had faced discrimination, so its leaders wanted acceptance in public life. The defeat of Al Smith, a Catholic, in the 1928 presidential election became the marker of that struggle, and it matters for John F. Kennedy later.

Ireland in the 1950s suffered heavy emigration and economic stagnation (no growth), and then turned to economic expansion. T. K. Whitaker drew up a programme for economic expansion in 1958, and Seán Lemass was Taoiseach (prime minister) from 1959 to 1966.

Assimilation means blending into the new country, and the chapter's other theme is keeping an Irish identity. Images, music and heritage links helped sustain Irishness among emigrants who were assimilating, because they gave them a shared picture of home.
notes.tip: Examiners reward answers that explain how images were created and then how they became links with the diaspora (Irish people living abroad). Keep both halves in mind as you read on.

notes.h: Stereotypes of the Irish in Hollywood
notes.b: Hollywood shaped the world's picture of Ireland, often through sentimental and comic stereotypes built on the older stage Irishman.
points: The stage Irishman was a 19th-century theatrical stereotype of the Irish as drunken, quick-tempered, sentimental and comic, and Hollywood inherited it, so the film image was an old caricature in a new medium.

Edward Harrigan and Tony Hart's Mulligan Guard comedies in New York in the 1870s and 1880s, and the Irish-American stage of Chauncey Olcott (a singer and actor popular in sentimental Irish plays around 1900), made the stage Irishman familiar to American audiences.

John Ford was an American director of Irish descent, born in Maine in 1894 to Irish immigrant parents whose families came from Spiddal, Co. Galway, and the Aran Islands. He made many films on Irish themes and Irish-American life.
Ford's The Informer, released in 1935 and set in Dublin during the revolutionary period, won him the Academy Award for Best Director.
Hollywood films often showed the Irish as rural, Catholic and emotional, and urban or industrial Ireland was rarely shown, so audiences abroad received a narrow picture of a modernising country.
Going My Way, released in 1944, presented an Irish-American priest in New York, and it became one of the popular images of Irish Catholicism in America.

Irish-American priests, policemen and fighting Irishmen became stock characters (familiar types that appear again and again), played by actors such as Pat O'Brien and the Dublin-born Barry Fitzgerald.
Disney's Darby O'Gill and the Little People (1959) presented Ireland as a land of leprechauns and banshees, which fixed a fairy-tale image for a mass audience.
notes.tip: Name a film with its date when you write about stereotypes. Do not mix up The Informer (1935) with The Quiet Man (1952), because they are two different Ford films.

notes.b: The Quiet Man was filmed in the west of Ireland in 1951 and released in 1952, and it became the most influential film image of rural Ireland. Its scenery turned a film image into a reason to travel.
points: The Quiet Man was directed by John Ford and starred John Wayne and Maureen O'Hara, with Barry Fitzgerald and Victor McLaglen. It was based on a story by the Irish writer Maurice Walsh.
It was filmed around Cong in Co. Mayo and in Connemara in 1951, with Ashford Castle as one of its main locations, and it was released in 1952.
The film won Academy Awards at the 1953 ceremony for Ford's direction and for the colour cinematography of Winton C. Hoch and Archie Stout.
The film's locations, including the Quiet Man Bridge in Cong, drew American visitors who wanted to see the places they had seen on screen.
The film helped to make Cong a tourist destination, and it shaped the expectations that many American visitors brought to Ireland.
Tourist interests welcomed the film's rural, comic, romantic Ireland, because it was attractive to American visitors, even though real Ireland in 1952 was suffering mass emigration.

Some critics objected that the film portrayed rural people as comic and drunken, and argued that it stereotyped Irish life. Contemporary Irish reaction was mixed and the film was popular, so the strongest criticism comes in later commentary.
notes.tip: Do not confuse the dates: filmed 1951, released 1952, Oscars at the 1953 ceremony. If asked about reactions, say some critics objected, not that Irish opinion was united.

notes.b: Maureen O'Hara was a Dublin-born actress who became a Hollywood star and was closely identified with spirited Irish heroines on screen. Her career shows how an Irish person helped to build the screen image of Ireland.
points: She was born Maureen FitzSimons in Ranelagh, Dublin, in 1920, and trained as an actress at the Abbey Theatre school in Dublin before her film career began in Britain and then moved to Hollywood.

Her breakthrough film was Jamaica Inn in 1939, a British production directed by Alfred Hitchcock in Britain. Her first Hollywood film was The Hunchback of Notre Dame, also in 1939, with Charles Laughton.
She appeared in How Green Was My Valley in 1941 and in Miracle on 34th Street in 1947, which established her as a major star.
She worked with John Ford on Rio Grande in 1950 and The Quiet Man in 1952, in which she played the fiery Mary Kate Danaher opposite John Wayne.

Her Dublin and Abbey training came first, and then the Hollywood studio system shaped her career by offering her the roles it chose, so she was both shaped by events and a participant in making the image.
Contemporary Irish-American audiences embraced her as an Irish star, while some Irish critics questioned whether her roles gave a true picture of Irish women.

Historians note that her screen image of the Irish woman as spirited and independent was partly a Hollywood creation, and that her career is an example of how Irish stars helped to build a screen Ireland.
She became a US citizen, received an honorary Academy Award in 2014, and died in 2015.
notes.tip: For a short profile give her birth name and birthplace (Ranelagh, 1920), Abbey Theatre training, Jamaica Inn 1939 under Hitchcock, a later film with its date, and The Quiet Man (1952) with Ford and John Wayne. Never call Jamaica Inn her first Hollywood film.

notes.b: Music carried Irish images to audiences abroad, from the sentimental songs and concert tenor of the early 20th century to the folk revival of the 1960s.
points: When Irish Eyes Are Smiling (1912) was an Irish-American stage song associated with Chauncey Olcott. Danny Boy had lyrics by the English lawyer and songwriter Frederic Weatherly in 1910, rewritten in 1913 to the air known as the Londonderry Air.
Sentimental songs of this kind gave an image of Ireland as a land of exile and longing, which suited emigrants who missed home.
John McCormack, a tenor born in Athlone in 1884, became famous in America and Britain and recorded Irish ballads. He died in 1945.
McCormack's concerts made Irish songs part of mainstream concert repertoire, and he was a leading figure in Irish-American cultural life.
Céilí bands (groups playing traditional Irish dance music for dancers) performed in Irish halls and clubs in America and Britain. They are not the same thing as the later folk revival.
Parish halls, clubs and dance halls kept Irish-American song and dance alive, and they gave emigrant communities a shared cultural life.
The Clancy Brothers, from Carrick-on-Suir, Co. Tipperary, and Tommy Makem, from Co. Armagh, became popular in America after appearing on the Ed Sullivan Show in 1961.

The folk revival (popular interest in traditional and ballad music in the late 1950s and 1960s) brought Irish songs to a young audience in America and Britain. It was led by the Clancy Brothers and, from 1962, the Dubliners, and it changed how Irish music was seen abroad.
notes.tip: In an essay, name a song or performer with a date. Keep McCormack (tenor), the Clancy Brothers (1960s folk) and the Dubliners (formed 1962) distinct, and do not describe Danny Boy as written to an Irish air in 1910.

notes.b: The Irish state promoted tourism to attract visitors, including descendants of emigrants who wanted to see the places their families had left. Each development has its own date, and examiners expect them.
points: Bord Fáilte, the Irish Tourist Board, was set up in 1952 under the Tourist Traffic Act to promote tourism and develop tourist facilities.
An Tóstal, a national festival of Irish culture and heritage, was launched in 1953 to draw visitors. It was a festival, whereas Bord Fáilte was a permanent body, so they are not the same thing.
Shannon Airport opened in 1945 as a transatlantic stop for aircraft, which brought American travellers through Ireland.
Shannon opened the world's first duty-free shop in 1947, which made it a point of contact between Irish life and travellers from America.
Aer Lingus began flights between Dublin, Shannon and New York in 1958, which made it easier for Irish Americans to visit.
Heritage tourism (travel to places of historical and cultural interest) grew in the 1950s and 1960s.
Roots tourism, the visiting of ancestral places by people of Irish descent, linked the Irish state's promotion of tourism with the emigrant communities abroad.
Tourism was valued as an export industry that brought in dollars and sterling, so it fitted the drive for economic growth of the late 1950s.
notes.tip: Give a date for each tourism development: Bord Fáilte 1952, An Tóstal 1953, Shannon 1945 and duty-free 1947, Aer Lingus 1958. Never describe An Tóstal and Bord Fáilte as the same thing.

notes.h: Other film images and film in Ireland
notes.b: Films about Ireland reached Irish audiences too, and Ireland had little film production of its own, so foreign productions and state censorship shaped the images on Irish screens.
points: Robert Flaherty's documentary Man of Aran (1934), by an American director, presented a romantic picture of life on the Aran Islands that many islanders did not recognise.
Carol Reed's film Odd Man Out (1947), set in Belfast and starring James Mason, showed the Irish revolutionary underworld to international audiences.
The Censorship of Films Act of 1923 gave the Irish state power to ban films, and the film censor (the official who judged films) removed or refused films on moral grounds.
Ardmore Studios opened at Bray, Co. Wicklow, in 1958 as the main film studio in Ireland.
Foreign productions, including Hollywood films, were shot in Ireland in the 1950s, and they brought Irish scenery and Irish actors to the screen.
Irish cinema-goers saw mostly Hollywood and British films, so the American image of Ireland reached Irish audiences as well as Americans.
notes.tip: Man of Aran (1934) and Odd Man Out (1947) are brief examples of other film images. Add them to a film answer with their dates.

notes.h: John F. Kennedy and Irish identity
notes.b: John F. Kennedy's election and his visit in 1963 changed how Irish Americans and the Irish public saw one another. Examiners want both sides, the USA and Ireland.
points: Kennedy's great-grandfather Patrick Kennedy left Dunganstown, Co. Wexford, in 1849. His mother, Rose, was a Fitzgerald, and her family was also of Irish descent.

Kennedy was elected in November 1960, becoming the first Catholic president of the United States. Many Irish Americans saw this as acceptance of Irish Catholics in public life, because Al Smith, a Catholic, had lost the 1928 election.
Kennedy visited Ireland from 26 to 29 June 1963, going to Dublin, Wexford (including Dunganstown), Cork, Galway and Limerick.
On 28 June 1963 he addressed the Oireachtas, the Irish parliament, in Dublin.
The visit drew large crowds and intense press coverage in Ireland, and it was widely celebrated as a moment of Irish pride.

Kennedy's image in Ireland combined ancestry with success in American politics, so it encouraged Irish people to think of their emigrant relatives as part of a shared story. For Irish America it confirmed that Irish Americans had arrived in American public life.
His assassination on 22 November 1963 was widely mourned in Ireland.
Historians argue that the visit fitted the self-confidence of Seán Lemass's government as the economy opened to the world, rather than causing it.
John F. Kennedy the president is a different person from his father Joe Kennedy, the ambassador, and from his great-grandfather Patrick Kennedy, who left in 1849.
notes.tip: Give dates: 1960, 26 to 29 June 1963 and 22 November 1963, plus Dunganstown in 1849. For a significance question, give a reason, not just the fact, and keep John's part distinct from Joe Kennedy's.

notes.b: Judging these images means weighing what they achieved against what they left out, and how people at the time saw them against how historians see them now.
points: Achievement: Hollywood films, music and tourism made Ireland widely known abroad, so they attracted visitors, brought in dollars and sterling and strengthened ties with emigrant descendants.
Limit: the images were often sentimental, rural and stereotyped, and they left out industrial and urban Ireland.
Contemporary view: tourism bodies and many audiences welcomed the images, while some critics objected that they stereotyped Irish people as comic or drunken.
Later view: historians see an Ireland made for export, and they debate how far the Kennedy visit changed Irish self-image or only celebrated it.
Film versus music: films fixed a rural, comic image, while the folk revival gave Irish culture a younger and more confident voice abroad.
notes.tip: Strong answers pair achievement with limit, and show that the images served Irish tourism interests and the emigrant's longing for home.
